\subsection{Actual coordinate curvature operator and Jacobi index bound}
\label{expanded:coordinate-curvature-operator}
Let $E$ be a real Hilbert space and let $\Gamma(x)$ be an actual continuously
bilinear map $E\times E\to E$. Regard $\Gamma$ as a field into the Banach
space of curried bounded bilinear maps. At a point $x$ where $\Gamma$ is
Fr\'echet differentiable, write $D\Gamma_x$ for its actual derivative. For
fixed $v$ define the bounded linear operator
\[
 \mathcal R_x(v)X=D\Gamma_x[X](v,v)-D\Gamma_x[v](X,v)
       +\Gamma_x(X,\Gamma_x(v,v))-\Gamma_x(v,\Gamma_x(X,v)).
\]
Each term is linear and continuous in $X$, and the operator is constructed
explicitly using curried-map flips and composition. It is the displayed
coordinate curvature expression $R(X,v)v$; identifying a supplied connection
field with the Levi-Civita connection of the frozen metric remains separate.
For total Lean functions the operator body uses actual \texttt{fderiv};
algebraic bounds remain valid on the total domain, while a
\texttt{HasFDerivAt} hypothesis identifies it with a genuine supplied derivative.
\label{expanded:coordinate-curvature-norm}
Bounded-map evaluation gives
$\|D\Gamma_x[X](v,v)\|\le\|D\Gamma_x\|\|X\|\|v\|^2$;
the permuted derivative term has the same bound. The two composition terms
are each at most $\|\Gamma_x\|^2\|X\|\|v\|^2$.
The triangle inequality therefore proves
\[
 \|\mathcal R_x(v)X\|\le
   2(\|D\Gamma_x\|+\|\Gamma_x\|^2)\|v\|^2\|X\|,
 \qquad
 \|\mathcal R_x(v)\|\le2(\|D\Gamma_x\|+\|\Gamma_x\|^2)\|v\|^2.
\]
If actual field and derivative bounds are $\|\Gamma_x\|\le C$ and
$\|D\Gamma_x\|\le D$, with $C,D\ge0$, this yields
$\|\mathcal R_x(v)\|\le2(D+C^2)\|v\|^2$. No desired curvature-operator
norm conclusion is supplied as a hypothesis.
\label{expanded:coordinate-curvature-jacobi-index}
Along an actual position $q(s)$ and velocity $v(s)$ on $[0,1]$, suppose
$\|\Gamma_{q(s)}\|\le C$, $\|D\Gamma_{q(s)}\|\le D$, and
$\|v(s)\|\le V$, where $C,D,V\ge0$.
Then the actual operator $\mathcal R_{q(s)}(v(s))$ is bounded by
$K=2(D+C^2)V^2$. If this operator field is continuous and the genuine
interval derivatives satisfy $Dj=j'$,
$Dj'=-r^2\mathcal R_{q(s)}(v(s))j(s)$, with $Kr^2\le1$,
the previously proved actual-operator Jacobi index estimate applies and yields
an error at most $2Kr^2\max(\|j(0)\|,\|j(1)\|)^2$.
Here both the curvature bound and the Jacobi index estimate are derived from
the actual supplied fields. The field bounds, differentiability/continuity,
parallel-frame realization, actual geodesic variation and distance-Hessian
identification remain explicit application obligations. This result supplies
neither a new literature premise nor a proof of the main theorem.
\label{expanded:coordinate-curvature-continuity}
Operator continuity can also be derived. Suppose the actual composed fields
$\Gamma(q(s))$, $D\Gamma_{q(s)}$ and $v(s)$ are continuous on $[0,1]$.
The flip of a bounded bilinear map is a linear isometry, so it preserves

operator terms and hence of $\mathcal R_{q(s)}(v(s))$. Thus the Jacobi index
estimate needs only these concrete field/derivative/velocity continuity

Their derivation from a smooth metric and a genuine geodesic remains a

\label{expanded:coordinate-curvature-transport}

$\|\widetilde{\mathcal R}\|\le A\,2(D+C^2)V^2 B$.
Continuity follows from continuity of $S,T$ and the derived coordinate

\section{Actual metric speed constancy and global velocity control}
\label{expanded:metric-geodesic-energy}
This is a supporting construction for the coordinate geodesics used in the
original shrinking-ball argument. It uses exactly a frozen admissible
Cartesian metric $g$ on $\mathbb R^3$, not an arbitrary independently supplied
inverse or metric-compatible connection. Put $M_g(x)X=g(x)X$ in the frozen
Euclidean vector norm, $Q_g=M_g^{-1}$, and let $\Gamma_g$ be the actual smooth
Koszul connection constructed earlier. Define the squared metric speed
\[
 e_g(q,v)(t)=\langle M_g(q(t))v(t),v(t)\rangle.
\]
It is a curve quantity, distinct from the frozen scalar-function Dirichlet
functional. Ordinary matrix multiplication and the real Euclidean inner
product give $\langle M_g(x)X,X\rangle=X^Tg(x)X$ exactly.

\paragraph{Constancy on an actual open interval.}
Let $q,v:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ satisfy genuine ambient derivatives
$q'(t)=v(t)$ and $v'(t)=-\Gamma_g(q(t))(v(t),v(t))$ at every point of
$I=(a,b)$. Metric compatibility and the already derived chain rule imply
$e'_g(t)=0$ at every such point. Hence $e_g$ is differentiable on $I$.
The real mean-value theorem on the convex, open, preconnected interval gives
$e_g(s)=e_g(t)$ for all $s,t\in I$. No constancy or minimizing property is
supplied as a hypothesis; no endpoint derivatives are required outside $I$.

\paragraph{An actual global quadratic lower bound.}
The scalar function $F(x,X)=\langle M_g(x)X,X\rangle$ is continuous.
On the compact set $\overline B(0,1)\times S(0,1)$ it is strictly positive,
because a unit vector is nonzero and the frozen $g(x)$ is positive definite.
Compactness gives $c>0$ with $c\le F(x,X)$ on this set. For arbitrary $X\ne0$
normalize by $\|X\|^{-1}$; bilinearity gives
$F(x,\|X\|^{-1}X)=\|X\|^{-2}F(x,X)$, hence
$c\|X\|^2\le F(x,X)$. At $X=0$ both sides vanish. Put
$\lambda=\min(c,1)>0$. For $\|x\|\le1$ the lower bound follows from
$\lambda\le c$. For $\|x\|\ge1$ the exact frozen exterior identity
$g(x)=I$ gives $F(x,X)=\|X\|^2$, and $\lambda\le1$ gives the same
bound. Thus $\lambda\|X\|^2\le F(x,X)$ for every $x,X$.

\paragraph{Velocity bound along the actual coordinate solution.}
Apply this global inequality at $x=q(t)$, $X=v(t)$, and substitute the
proved interval constancy at any initial time $s\in I$. Then
\[
 \lambda\|v(t)\|^2\le e_g(q,v)(s),\qquad
 \|v(t)\|^2\le e_g(q,v)(s)/\lambda\quad(t\in I).
\]
Positivity of $\lambda$ justifies the division. This supplies a bound for a
fixed actual admissible metric and supplied genuine local solutions. It does
not assert global flow existence, smooth initial-data dependence, normal or
minimizing neighborhoods, parallel frames, Jacobi realization, a distance
Hessian, or constants uniform over the manuscript's shrinking metric family.
Those applications remain explicit obligations. No published result enters as
an unproved premise, and the frozen main type and definitions are unchanged.

\hypertarget{source-e4785d68ade7-concrete-directional-differential-and-weighted-derivative-operators}{%
\subsection{Concrete directional differential and weighted derivative
operators}\label{source-e4785d68ade7-concrete-directional-differential-and-weighted-derivative-operators}}

For a finite coordinate type sigma, let F(p,q)=sum\_alpha alpha!
p\_alpha q\_alpha, exactly the canonical Fischer inner product. Define
W\_f(q)=sum\_i f\_i q\_i using scalar polynomial multiplication C(f\_i),
and a\_f(v)=W\_f(partial\_i v). These are actual polynomial operators,
not norm variables. All real scalars f\_i are permitted; B=sum\_i
f\_i\^{}2 \textgreater=0.

Prove F(W\_f q,W\_f q) \textless= B sum\_i F(q\_i,q\_i). If
B\textgreater0, expand the nonnegative expression sum\_i
F(q\_i-C(f\_i/B)W\_f q,q\_i-C(f\_i/B)W\_f q). Its cross term is F(W\_f
q,W\_f q), by proven Fischer bilinearity, and its scalar-square term is
B times that same square. The expression is Q-B\^{}\{-1\}S
\textgreater=0; multiplying by B proves the assertion. If B=0, each
f\_i=0 and W\_f q=0, so no inverse issue is hidden.

For actual homogeneous v of degree k, the canonical Euler/Fischer
identity gives sum\_i F(partial\_i v,partial\_i v)=k F(v,v).
Substitution proves F(a\_f v,a\_f v)\textless=k B F(v,v). Under actual
gradient smallness sum\_i f\_i\^{}2 \textless= beta\^{}2, this yields
the source\textquotesingle s bound k beta\^{}2 F(v,v). This hypothesis
is a source profile condition; coercivity is not hypothesized.

For a supplied vector polynomial w\_i (interpreted as base covariant
derivative at a point, interpretation still open), define D\_i\^{}+
v=w\_i+C(k f\_i)v and D\_i\^{}-v=-w\_i+C(k f\_i)v. Then their divergence
sum obeys div(D\^{}+v)+div(D\^{}-v)=C(2k)a\_f v. Expand
div(D\^{}+v)=-div(D\^{}-v)+C(2k)a\_f v. Positivity of the squared norm
of the difference yields
\textbar\textbar p+q\textbar\textbar\_F\^{}2\textless=2\textbar\textbar p\textbar\textbar\_F\^{}2+2\textbar\textbar q\textbar\textbar\_F\^{}2.
Together with the directional contraction this proves F(div D\^{}+,div
D\^{}+)\textless=2 F(div D\^{}-,div D\^{}-)+8 k\^{}3 beta\^{}2 F(v,v).
If each w\_i is homogeneous of degree k, the established divergence
contraction supplies the other bound (k+n-1) sum\_i
F(D\_i\^{}+,D\_i\^{}+). Multiply the two derived inequalities by 1-zeta
and zeta, for 0\textless=zeta\textless=1, and add to prove exactly the
pointwise convex bound. This is a genuine actual-operator instance of
the source pointwise step, independent of unproved base integration
identities.

\hypertarget{source-e4785d68ade7-infinite-degree-coefficient-families}{%
\subsection{Infinite degree coefficient
families}\label{source-e4785d68ade7-infinite-degree-coefficient-families}}

normalization (finite product). With n\textgreater0 each
N\_k\textgreater0. Define normalized square E\_k(p)=F(p,p)/N\_k;
normalized vector square is its coordinate sum. Families remain explicit
functions from N to polynomials; no unproved identification with sphere
L2 is claimed. On q(k) homogeneous degree k+1, actual lowering is div
q(k) in degree k, with E\_k(div q(k)) \textless= (k+n)(n+2k) sum\_i
E\_\{k+1\}(q(k)\emph{i). For harmonic q(k), actual sphere-normalized
raising is C(n+2(k+1)) harmonicRaising(k) q(k), with E}\{k+2\}(raised
q(k)) \textless= (n+2(k+1))(k+2) sum\_i E\_\{k+1\}(q(k)\_i). The upper
bound uses the exact harmonic-raising norm identity and finite mixed
contraction bound, discarding only its nonnegative correction term.

For any nonnegative degree weight omega\_k and a summable right-hand
weighted energy, summability of the actual output squares follows from
the nonnegative comparison theorem; monotonicity of tsum proves the
infinite-family energy inequality. The operator square energy is an
actual infinite sum of factorial-weighted coefficient expressions, so
this removes a finite-only algebra restriction. This does not establish
a completed Hilbert domain or smooth sphere convergence.

For harmonic h of degree k+2, F(harmonicRaising(k)q,h)=sum\_i
F(q\_i,partial\_i h), since its radius-square correction pairs to zero.
The normalization recursion cancels the raising scalar, proving
E-pairing adjoint identity exactly between degrees k+1 and k+2;
corresponding termwise infinite series equality follows by tsum
congruence (a Hilbert adjoint assertion additionally needs
domain/density control).

\hypertarget{source-bf1ada3d0e91-source-and-exact-conventions}{%
\subsection{Source and exact
conventions}\label{source-bf1ada3d0e91-source-and-exact-conventions}}

Original sections 03/04/05/06 have been read, including actual cross
existence, Green flux and local harmonicity, moving trace expansion,
mixed base-angular coercivity and bootstrap parameter order. The current
full expansion is expanded/calderon-ball-expanded-v009.tex, especially
angular-expanded:trace and fixed-separation-supp:limits. No Green
continuation, density bound, metric uniqueness or complete
pseudodifferential estimate is assumed here.

The first equation is Delta\_g u=0 (positive Cartesian principal part);
its Green inverse is -Delta\_g. The reference gamma=exp(-2 L t0)g has
the same solution equation after multiplication by exp(2 L t0):

\begin{verbatim}
L_gamma = Delta_gamma + (n-2)L <dt0,du>_gamma.
\end{verbatim}

Thus in gamma-normal coordinates at y the principal first radius
derivative vanishes and the drift at the center is b(y)=(n-2)L
grad\_gamma t0(y). For n=3 it is L grad\_gamma t0(y). After
x=exp\_y\^{}gamma(r z) and multiplication by r², the family is

\begin{verbatim}
L_(y,r) = Delta_z + r b(y) dot grad_z + r² R_(y,r).
\end{verbatim}

The smooth remainder includes both second-order metric terms and
first-order drift variation. There is no zero-order potential. The
radial trace is the outward radial derivative on the unit sphere, not
the conormal operator on the physical first-metric ball.

\hypertarget{source-bf1ada3d0e91-complete-first-variation-proof}{%
\subsection{Complete first-variation
proof}\label{source-bf1ada3d0e91-complete-first-variation-proof}}

Fix a harmonic homogeneous polynomial v of degree k \textgreater=1, and
set q=b dot grad v. Commutation of Cartesian derivatives gives Delta
q=0; Euler homogeneity gives degree(q)=k-1. Set d=2k+n-2\textgreater0
and

\begin{verbatim}
w(z)=(1-|z|²) q(z)/(2 d).
\end{verbatim}

The radius-square product rule gives Delta((1-\textbar z\textbar²)q)=-2d
q, so Delta w=-q. On \textbar z\textbar=1, w=0. These are the
inhomogeneous equation and boundary condition of the first radius
derivative of the genuine Dirichlet solution: differentiating L\_r
v\_r=0 and the fixed boundary data gives Delta v\textquotesingle\_0=-b
dot grad v, v\textquotesingle\_0\textbar sphere=0. Standard Dirichlet
uniqueness identifies v\textquotesingle\_0=w; identification with a true
family requires the explicit standard inverse/differentiability
interface, and will not be asserted as a formal consequence of
polynomial identities alone.

Its radial trace is z dot grad w=-q/d on the unit sphere. Consequently

\begin{verbatim}
B1 v= - b dot A v / (2k+n-2).
\end{verbatim}

For k=0, q=0 and w=B1v=0. For k=1, q=b dot a is constant for v=a dot z;
w=(1-\textbar z\textbar²)(b dot a)/(2n), B1v=-(b dot a)/n. In dimension
three the denominator is 2k+1, and the degree-one trace is -b dot a/3.
This fixes sign, dimension and normalization.

\hypertarget{source-bf1ada3d0e91-explicit-operator-identity-and-complete-order-zero-first-correction}{%
\subsection{Explicit operator identity and complete order-zero first
correction}\label{source-bf1ada3d0e91-explicit-operator-identity-and-complete-order-zero-first-correction}}

There is a second construction that identifies the entire first
correction, rather than only its Sobolev norm. For the constant center
drift model L\_r=Delta+r b dot grad, put u=exp(-r b dot z/2)v. Direct
differentiation gives

\begin{verbatim}
L_r u=exp(-r b dot z/2)(Delta-r²|b|²/4)v.
\end{verbatim}

Its radial Dirichlet trace is therefore exactly

\begin{verbatim}
Lambda_r=M_exp(-r b.omega/2) Lambda_Helmholtz(r²|b|²/4)
         M_exp(r b.omega/2) - r M_(b.omega)/2.
\end{verbatim}

At r=0 the Helmholtz operator is B; the potential depends on r², so its
first radius derivative is zero whenever the usual differentiable
Dirichlet inverse interface is supplied. Thus

\begin{verbatim}
B1=(1/2)[B,M_(b.omega)]-(1/2)M_(b.omega).
\end{verbatim}

This agrees with the forcing formula. Indeed the boundary multiplication
of a degree-k harmonic v has raising part
(b.z)v-\textbar z\textbar²(b.Av)/d and lowering part (b.Av)/d, with
d=2k+n-2. The former is harmonic of degree k+1 by the radius-square
Laplacian identity, and the latter has degree k-1. Applying B to each
and subtracting the multiplication gives precisely -b.Av/d. This formula
handles k=0 as well because {[}B,M{]}1=M1.

Given the standard Euclidean B in Psi\^{}1 and the standard scalar
angular commutator rule, this expression is in the complete Psi\^{}0
topology, with smooth kernels included. The center dependence is only
through smooth b and orthonormal trivialization. This identifies the
required first correction using an actual PDE gauge transformation; it
does not prove the second Taylor remainder in complete Psi\^{}1 topology
for the variable metric family. That remaining remainder is exactly the
standard parameter-dependent Dirichlet-calculus obligation, not a novel
transfer bound.

\hypertarget{source-bf1ada3d0e91-degree-uniform-strength-and-actual-derivative-budget}{%
\subsection{Degree-uniform strength and actual derivative
budget}\label{source-bf1ada3d0e91-degree-uniform-strength-and-actual-derivative-budget}}

The Fischer-to-probability-sphere factor is N\_k=n(n+2)...(n+2k-2).
Euler and Fischer adjunction give sum\_i F(A\_i v,A\_i v)=k F(v,v);
N\_k/N\_(k-1)=d. Hence sum\_i \textbar\textbar A\_i
v\textbar\textbar²\_sphere=k d
\textbar\textbar v\textbar\textbar²\_sphere. Cauchy-Schwarz gives

\begin{verbatim}
||B1 v||²_sphere <= |b|² k/d ||v||²_sphere <= (|b|²/2)||v||²_sphere  (n>=2).
\end{verbatim}

For an H\^{}s fiber norm the output degree k-1 has weight k\^{}(2s) and
the input weight (k+1)\^{}(2s). The ratio is bounded by
2\^{}(2\textbar s\textbar), proving B1:H\^{}s-\textgreater H\^{}s for
each real s, uniformly in degree. Finite sums extend by density. Proving
the exact sphere/Fischer integration correspondence remains separate;
the separate angular-functional-author packet proves the explicit
Fischer normalization and summable all-degree coefficient-energy bound;
its sphere integration correspondence remains a separate obligation.
This radial packet does not silently call Fischer energy the sphere
norm.

B1 is linear in b. Every base derivative at fixed orthonormal
trivialization is the same multiplier with the corresponding derivative
of b, plus bounded frame connection terms. Through six base derivatives
it therefore uses only the corresponding fixed first-metric/conformal
background derivatives, with no h derivative and no radius derivative.
The first correction is order zero by this explicit spectral
computation. This proves Sobolev mapping control; it does not by itself
prove the complete classical symbol and smoothing-kernel topology
required by the source commutator calculus.

For r=r\_delta, the contribution f\_i r B1 lies in the bounded
order-zero remainder since r beta \textless= epsilon/beta. Its jth base
derivatives require derivatives of f through j+1 and radius through j:
\textbar partial\^{}a r\textbar\textless=C\_a r beta\^{}a and
\textbar partial\^{}a f\_i\textbar\textless=C\_a beta\^{}(a+1), so
\textbar partial\^{}j(r f\_i)\textbar\textless=C\_j r
beta\^{}(j+1)\textless=C\_j epsilon beta\^{}(j-1). Thus j\textless=6
consumes f through7, within source8. Angular differentiation acts on A
and the degree multiplier, not on h. Products with normalized
second-metric coefficients use h through at most8 as already stated in

\subsection{Cutoff and remaining original

\hypertarget{source-71285ede3265-coordinate-model-and-source-coefficient-classes}{%
\subsection{Coordinate model and source coefficient
classes}\label{source-71285ede3265-coordinate-model-and-source-coefficient-classes}}

Use a fixed finite orthonormal trivialization of the tangent sphere
bundle. The sphere probability measure is fixed there; base measure is
mu(y)dy with mu\textgreater0 smooth, bounded above and below, and fixed
smooth background bounds. Horizontal differentiation is partial\_i plus
a fixed angular first-order connection operator. Replacing it by
partial\_i contributes only the lower base orders included below.

Write the actual normalized trace decomposition P=2T+U+J as

\begin{verbatim}
T^dagger = K^l partial_l + M,
U = a^{ij} partial_i partial_j + B^i partial_i + C,
Z = T^flat - T^dagger,
a^{ij}=r Q^{ij}=a^{ji} real scalar, angular independent.
\end{verbatim}

The reference raising coefficient has K\^{}l in Psi\^{}1 with fixed
smooth base bounds. M is in beta Psi\^{}2. Z is in beta Psi\^{}1. With j
base derivatives, these have allowances K: fixed background (or the
weaker beta\^{}j), M: beta\^{}(j+1), Z: beta\^{}(j+1). The U
coefficients obey

\begin{verbatim}
partial^j a in epsilon beta^(j-2) Psi^0,
partial^j B in epsilon beta^(j-1) Psi^1,
partial^j C in epsilon beta^j Psi^2.
\end{verbatim}

Only the finitely many derivatives counted below are needed. Psi means
scalar classical angular operators with the complete symbol and
smoothing seminorms sufficient for the indicated Sobolev mappings. For
scalar angular A in Psi\^{}m and D in Psi\^{}n, {[}A,D{]} is in
Psi\^{}(m+n-1). In particular, this rule applies to K,B,M,C: they are
scalar operators on sphere functions, despite carrying a coordinate
tensor index. It would not hold for an arbitrary matrix-valued angular
principal symbol.

These classes are derived from the actual C\_i\^{}*=r\^{}-1
A\_i\^{}*+f\_i B+E\_i+F\_i, E\_i in r Psi\^{}1, F\_i in Psi\^{}0, with
six allowed base derivatives. The normalized second equation has no
ordinary coordinate drift (harmonic coordinates); in the gamma
connection its drift is b\_2\^{}k=Q\^{}\{ij\}Gamma\_gamma\^{}k\_ij.
Consequently its derivatives do not cost an extra derivative of h.

The coefficient a is exactly rQ. The first-base coefficient consists of
2rQ f B, 2h A\^{}*, 2rQ(E+F), r b\_2, and the fixed horizontal
connection terms; its size is epsilon beta\^{}-1 Psi\^{}1. The zero-base
term has (h/r)A\^{}*A\^{}*, rQ(f\_i f\_j B²+f\_\{j;i\}B), and products
with E/F and drift. Cross products A\^{}*F and b\_2 A\^{}* have uniform
order one and are assigned to J. The others have size epsilon Psi\^{}2.
The derivative of r\^{}-1 cancels the degree shift
{[}B,A\^{}*{]}=A\^{}*; this cancellation is exact and is required to
identify 2T.

For each j used here, Leibniz and the source profile yield

\begin{verbatim}
|partial^j r| <= C_j r beta^j,
|partial^j(r^-1)| <= C_j r^-1 beta^j,
|partial^j(h/r)| <= C_j epsilon beta^j,
r beta² <= epsilon, beta>=1.
\end{verbatim}

Angular differentiation does not differentiate h(y). Fixed angular
symbol regularity is supplied by the first metric, not by infinitely
many small h derivatives.

\hypertarget{source-71285ede3265-exact-commutator-expansion-with-no-third-base-derivative}{%
\subsection{Exact commutator expansion with no third base
derivative}\label{source-71285ede3265-exact-commutator-expansion-with-no-third-base-derivative}}

In the following formulas products and commutators are genuine ordered
angular operator products. Coefficient derivatives are ordinary base
derivatives. Summation is understood, and a is symmetric.

For H=K\^{}l partial\_l+M, direct Leibniz expansion gives {[}H,U{]} as
the following seven groups:

\begin{verbatim}
[K partial, a partial²]
  = K^l(partial_l a^{ij}) partial_i partial_j
    -2a^{ij}(partial_i K^l) partial_j partial_l
    -a^{ij}(partial_i partial_j K^l) partial_l.

[K partial, B partial]
  = [K^l,B^i] partial_l partial_i
    +K^l(partial_l B^i) partial_i
    -B^i(partial_i K^l) partial_l.

[K partial, C]
  = [K^l,C] partial_l + K^l(partial_l C).

[M,a partial²]
  = -2a^{ij}(partial_i M) partial_j
    -a^{ij}(partial_i partial_j M).

[M,B partial]
  = [M,B^i] partial_i - B^i(partial_i M).

[M,C] = [M,C].
\end{verbatim}

There is no unlisted {[}M,a{]}partial² term because a is angular
independent. The cubic base term in the first line is (K\^{}l
a\^{}\{ij\}-a\^{}\{ij\}K\^{}l)partial\_l partial\_i partial\_j=0. This
is exact cancellation, not a bound that loses a base derivative.

The second-base coefficients are in epsilon beta\^{}-1 Psi\^{}1: K
partial a has that size, a partial K is smaller, and {[}K,B{]} loses one
angular order. The first-base coefficients are in epsilon Psi\^{}2: K
partial B, B partial K, {[}K,C{]}, a partial M and {[}M,B{]} all satisfy
this. The zero-base coefficients are in epsilon beta Psi\^{}3: K partial
C, a partial²M, B partial M and {[}M,C{]} satisfy it, with lower angular
orders included by Sobolev embedding. The first base derivative of a
second-base coefficient is in epsilon Psi\^{}1, which is exactly what
the one integration by parts requires.

\hypertarget{source-71285ede3265-the-adjoint-difference-and-quadratic-perturbation}{%
\subsection{The adjoint difference and quadratic
perturbation}\label{source-71285ede3265-the-adjoint-difference-and-quadratic-perturbation}}

Sphere adjoints are stars. Since a is real, angular independent and
symmetric, integration by parts gives exactly

\begin{verbatim}
V := U^dagger-U = D^i partial_i + E,
D^i = 2 mu^-1 partial_j(mu a^{ij}) - B^i - (B^i)^*,
E = mu^-1 partial_i partial_j(mu a^{ij})
    -mu^-1 partial_i(mu (B^i)^*) + C^* - C.
\end{verbatim}

Hence D is in epsilon beta\^{}-1 Psi\^{}1 and E is in epsilon Psi\^{}2.
There is no second-base part in V. This is the precise use of reality of
rQ; angular independence alone would not cancel the leading adjoint part
of a complex coefficient.

Now {[}U\^{}dagger,U{]}={[}V,U{]}. Substituting K=D,M=E into the
previous exact expansion proves no third base derivative and the
stronger classes

\begin{verbatim}
base2: epsilon² beta^-2 Psi^1,
base1: epsilon² beta^-1 Psi^2,
base0: epsilon² Psi^3.
\end{verbatim}

They lie in the required epsilon² beta\^{}-1 Psi\^{}1, epsilon² Psi\^{}2
and epsilon² beta Psi\^{}3 since beta\textgreater=1. A derivative of its
base2 coefficient remains controlled by epsilon² beta\^{}-1 Psi\^{}1.
There is no concealed fourth base derivative.

For UZ the exact expansion is

\begin{verbatim}
UZ = a^{ij}Z partial_i partial_j
     +(2a^{ij}partial_i Z+B^j Z) partial_j
     +a^{ij}partial_i partial_j Z+B^i partial_i Z+CZ.
\end{verbatim}

Its classes are respectively epsilon beta\^{}-1 Psi\^{}1, epsilon
Psi\^{}2, and epsilon beta Psi\^{}3. Its adjoint can be treated in the
quadratic pairing without expanding additional derivatives.

The source error operator is

\begin{verbatim}
E_err = 2[H,U] + 2[H,U]^dagger + [V,U]
        -2(UZ+(UZ)^dagger).
\end{verbatim}

The equality {[}U\^{}dagger,T{]}={[}T\^{}dagger,U{]}\^{}dagger is exact.
In its real quadratic form, the adjoint partners have the same real
part. Thus it suffices to estimate the displayed operators themselves;
no additional base derivatives are consumed by writing out those
partners.

\hypertarget{source-71285ede3265-actual-mixed-sobolev-form-bound}{%
\subsection{Actual mixed Sobolev form
bound}\label{source-71285ede3265-actual-mixed-sobolev-form-bound}}

Let phi be smooth, compactly supported in the base, with arbitrary
angular degree; the zero-mean condition is needed only for the
subsequent raising estimate. Define

\begin{verbatim}
X=||partial phi||_(H^(1/2)),  Y=||phi||_(H^(3/2)).
\end{verbatim}

For a second-base term S\^{}\{ij\}partial\_i partial\_j with S in
epsilon beta\^{}-1 Psi\^{}1, one integration by parts against mu dy
gives

\begin{verbatim}
-<S^{ij}partial_j phi, partial_i phi>
-<mu^-1 partial_i(mu S^{ij})partial_j phi,phi>.
\end{verbatim}

The first is bounded by C epsilon beta\^{}-1 X² pointwise in y, using
Psi\^{}1:H\^{}(1/2)-\textgreater H\^{}(-1/2). The differentiated
coefficient is epsilon Psi\^{}1, so the second is bounded by C epsilon X
Y (a stronger angular norm on phi is allowed). First-base epsilon
Psi\^{}2 terms map H\^{}(1/2)-\textgreater H\^{}(-3/2), and are bounded
by the same C epsilon X Y. Zero-base epsilon beta Psi\^{}3 terms map
H\^{}(3/2)-\textgreater H\^{}(-3/2), and are bounded by C epsilon beta
Y².

Pointwise weighted Young gives 2XY\textless=beta\^{}-1 X²+beta Y².
Integrating in y therefore proves

\begin{verbatim}
|Re<E_err phi,phi>| <= C epsilon integral(beta^-1 X²+beta Y²)
                     <= C epsilon N(phi)²,
\end{verbatim}

for epsilon\textless=1. Constants are independent of delta, even when
beta is unbounded above. No base Fourier cutoff, bound on partial² phi,
estimate on its third derivatives, or comparison of base and angular
frequencies has been inserted. These are exactly the mixed strengths
retained by the source raising estimate.

In coordinates partial differs from the horizontal nabla by an angular
Psi\^{}1 operator with fixed bounded coefficients. Then

\begin{verbatim}
beta^-1||partial phi||_(1/2)²
  <=2 beta^-1||nabla phi||_(1/2)²+C beta^-1||phi||_(3/2)²,
\end{verbatim}

and the latter term is controlled by
beta\textbar\textbar phi\textbar\textbar\_(3/2)². A fixed finite base
partition produces first and zero order errors with the same classes.
Thus the coordinate estimate is the claimed intrinsic form bound.

\hypertarget{source-71285ede3265-explicit-finite-derivative-budget}{%
\subsection{Explicit finite derivative
budget}\label{source-71285ede3265-explicit-finite-derivative-budget}}

The longest path through the quadratic perturbation is a coefficient a
differentiated twice in E=V\_0, then once in {[}D partial,U{]} or twice
in {[}E,a partial²{]}, and finally once when a second-base coefficient
is integrated by parts. Inspecting actual terms sharpens the count:
{[}E,a partial²{]} has at most first base order, so it is NOT integrated
by parts. It uses at most four base derivatives of a. The second-base
coefficients from {[}D partial,U{]} are D partial a, a partial D and
{[}D,B{]}; their final derivative uses a through order3 and B through
order2. The other first/zero coefficients use a through4, B through3 and
C through2 at most. For {[}H,U{]}, the analogous maxima are a through2,
B through2, C through1; M and K are fixed first-metric/profile
quantities. UZ requires Z through2 and U through1 if its second-base
term is differentiated. All maxima are within the source allowance of
five U coefficient derivatives.

Constructing C includes one derivative of a trace remainder S\_i. Taking
C through order2 needs S\_i through3; the conservative
five-coefficient-derivative envelope would need S\_i through6. Thus the
source\textquotesingle s six trace derivatives suffice. Those trace
coefficients contain f\_i, so their sixth base derivative uses f
through7. h enters only as h/r, h A\^{}*, Q and b\_2=Q Gamma; five
coefficient derivatives need h through5, while a deliberately
conservative budget of four error derivatives plus one construction
derivative plus two trace/profile allowances stays below8. No angular
symbol derivative hits h. Fixed first-metric derivatives can be higher
and remain background bounds; they are not asserted to obey epsilon r
smallness.

\hypertarget{source-71285ede3265-result-and-precise-remaining-obligations}{%
\subsection{Result and precise remaining
obligations}\label{source-71285ede3265-result-and-precise-remaining-obligations}}

At the mathematical authoring level, the mixed error form follows from
the actual scalar trace coefficient classes, the reality/angular
independence of rQ, and standard angular scalar calculus. The explicit
formulas show why the high base frequencies do not cause a loss and why
the eight small derivatives of h suffice. No admissible quasimode or
failure was found in this comparison. This is not a claim that the
entire section05 or main theorem has been proved.

Remaining: formal realization of the complete parameter-dependent scalar
sphere Psi algebra and Sobolev mappings; exact trace Taylor remainder
including smoothing topology; genuine weighted raising estimate on the
curved sphere bundle; full source Green continuation/local harmonicity
and cutoff trace bounds; reviewed published interfaces and kernel
checking. The explicit PDE trace packet is independently useful and
formally compiled separately.

\section{Radial forcing and trace in the exact frozen Euclidean space}
\label{expanded:green-euclidean-realization}
The preceding evaluated polynomial proof uses finite Cartesian functions
with their Pi norm. Here we transfer it to the exact frozen
$\mathbb R^3=\operatorname{EuclideanSpace}\mathbb R(\operatorname{Fin}3)$;
we do not replace that space or its norm. Let
$C:\mathbb R^3\simeq_L\mathbb R^{\{0,1,2\}}$ be the checked
\texttt{PiLp.continuousLinearEquiv} with exponent two. Its underlying
map is the coordinate function and $C(e_i)$ is the ordinary single-coordinate
vector. For a finite polynomial $p$ define
$P_p(x)=\operatorname{eval}(Cx,p)$.

The genuine Fr\'echet chain rule gives
$DP_p(x)=D\operatorname{eval}_p(Cx)\circ C$.
Thus $DP_p(x)[v]=\sum_i v_i\operatorname{eval}(Cx,\partial_i p)$.
Applying this to the actual frozen coordinate derivative
$d_iP_p(x)=DP_p(x)[e_i]$ gives exactly
$d_iP_p(x)=P_{\partial_i p}(x)$. Applying the same identity once more
and summing gives the true Cartesian Laplacian
$\sum_i d_i(d_iP_p)(x)=P_{\Delta_{\rm pol}p}(x)$.
Every derivative here is an actual total Fr\'echet derivative in the
unchanged frozen norm.

The Euclidean square-norm identity is
$\|x\|^2=\sum_i x_i^2$. Hence $\|x\|=1$ implies the sphere equation
used by the evaluated polynomial proof. For harmonic homogeneous $p$ of
degree $k\ge1$ and $b\in\mathbb R^3$, its explicit drift response
$W=P_{\mathrm{driftFirstVariation}(k,Cb,p)}$ has
\[
 \sum_i d_i(d_iW)(x)=-DP_p(x)[b],\qquad
 W(x)=0\quad(\|x\|=1),
\]
by substitution into the already proved formal Laplacian and forcing
identities. On that same actual Euclidean sphere the chain rule and the
proved radial formula give
\[
 DW(x)[x]=-(2k+1)^{-1}DP_p(x)[b].
\]
For the coordinate polynomial $p=z_j$, the right side is $-b_j/3$;
constant polynomials have zero response. These are genuine frozen-coordinate
PDE and outward radial derivative identities. They do not yet identify the
explicit response with the derivative of a variable-metric Dirichlet solution
family, a conormal trace, or a full uniform Green-transfer estimate. Those
standard inverse/parameter and original analytic applications remain open.

\hypertarget{source-e1387282d54f-abstract-bundled-bilinear-route-before-lean-2026-10-09-0048-utc}{%
\subsection{7. Abstract bundled bilinear route (before Lean, 2026-10-09
00:48
UTC)}\label{source-e1387282d54f-abstract-bundled-bilinear-route-before-lean-2026-10-09-0048-utc}}

Let V be a real normed vector space, W a real Hilbert space, i:W→V a
bounded linear inclusion, B:V×V→R a bounded bilinear form, and B0:W×W→R
a bounded bilinear form with explicit representation B0(w,v)=B(iw,iv).
Assume B0 coercive. The affine forcing for datum d∈V is ℓ(v)=−B(d,iv), a
continuous linear functional because it is the negative of composition
of B(d,·) with i. Let w0=B0\^{}\{-1\}ℓ via the existing checked
IsCoercive.solutionOfFunctional API, and U=d+iw0. That API gives
B0(w0,v)=ℓ(v). Thus B(iw0,iv)=−B(d,iv), and bilinearity yields B(U,iv)=0
for every v. This orthogonality statement needs neither symmetry nor
ellipticity beyond the already supplied coercivity of B0.

Assume separately B symmetric. For any v∈W, bilinear expansion gives
\begin{align*}B(U+iv,U+iv)&=B(U,U)+B(U,iv)\\ &\quad+B(iv,U)+B(iv,iv).\end{align*} Orthogonality and symmetry
set the two cross terms to0. The representation turns the last term into
B0(v,v). Coercivity implies B0(v,v)≥0. Given arbitrary affine competitor
d+iv, use z=v−w0 and linearity of i to identify d+iv=U+iz; consequently
B(U,U)≤B(d+iv,d+iv). This is the actual attained affine minimum, with no
smooth density premise. Smooth-density is used only later in the
separately passed exact frozen infimum correspondence.

Specialization: V is the actual Tau W1p volume ballOpens2, W its actual
W1p0, i the subtype continuous linear map, B the bundled energyFormH1L,
B0 the bundled energyFormH1L0. Prove the representation through the
published checked equality lemmas energyFormH1L0\_apply and
energyFormH1L\_apply, with explicit arguments rather than rewriting
integrated energy definitions. Convert final equalities through those
same evaluation lemmas only once. The actual drift/mass functions are
zero functions; normalize them explicitly and never conflate scalar0
with a function at an unresolved type. Tau has global shortcut
seminormed/normed-space instances plus local
normed-group/inner-product-space W1p0 instances: specialization must
register the exact local W1p0 instances expected by
IsCoercive.solutionOfFunctional; abstract lemmas quantify the structures
once, avoiding repeated reconstruction of nested Sobolev graph spaces.

This route changes proof organization only. It adds no mathematical
premise, changes no frozen definition or target, and remains private
development until actual compilation and root\textquotesingle s
canonical current-input checks.

# All-order normalized softplus jets — expanded proof v001

Authority: original manuscript §4, Lemma `balls:profiles`, formula for A and the assertion |A^(j)| ≤ C_j A^(j+1); §5 `angular:profile-bounds` through order eight. The chosen departure replaces endpoint asymptotic differentiation by a finite monomial recurrence and elementary inequalities. No new literature premise is used. The fixed frozen v002 target and canonical source remain unchanged.

## J1. Dimensionless variables and true derivatives
For z ∈ ℝ put q(z)=exp(z)/(1+exp(z)), w(z)=1/(1+exp(z)), and L(z)=log(1+exp(z)). Then 0<q,w<1, q+w=1, L>0, w=exp(-L). Actual scalar derivatives are q'=qw, w'=-qw, L'=q. Consequently the actual derivative of H(z)=log L(z) is A(z)=q/L. Here H is smooth because L is strictly positive.

## J2. Exact finite recurrence
Let a term be c q^a w^b L^d with real coefficient c and natural exponents a,b,d. At order j, interpret the term as c q^a w^b L^d/L^j. Its actual derivative is the sum of three terms at order j+1:

* coefficient c a, exponents (a,b+1,d+1);
* coefficient -c b, exponents (a+1,b,d+1);
* coefficient c(d-j), exponents (a+1,b,d).

This identity follows by the ordinary product, quotient and natural-power derivative rules and q'=qw,w'=-qw,L'=q. All denominators are nonzero. Start at j=1 with the single term q. Concatenate the three replacements at every step. Thus the resulting finite polynomial P_j satisfies H^(j)=P_j/L^j for every j≥1. No arbitrary derivative function or desired jet estimate is assumed.

## J3. Invariants of nonzero terms
At order j every nonzero coefficient term satisfies a+d≥j and d>0⇒b>0. The initial q term satisfies these. The first replacement raises d and b, while the second either has b>0 or coefficient zero. The third keeps d and b. Each replacement increases a+d by at least one. Zero coefficient terms can be retained and excluded from the invariant condition; no cancellation assumption is needed.

## J4. Uniform monomial bound
For q≤1/2, log(1+exp z)≤exp z=q/w≤2q. Also q,w≤1. Thus q^a w^b L^d≤2^d q^(a+d)≤2^d q^j.

For q≥1/2 and d=0 the monomial is≤1≤2^j q^j. For d>0 the invariant gives b≥1, hence q^a w^b L^d≤w L^d=exp(-L)L^d≤d!, using the d-th nonnegative Taylor term of exp(L). Therefore it is≤2^j d! q^j. The common deliberately nonsharp bound 2^(d+j) d! q^j covers both cases. The finite sum of the absolute coefficients times these constants bounds |P_j| by C_j q^j. It follows that |H^(j)|≤C_j A^j. C_j depends only on j, never on z, delta, the radius multiplier, or the exponent p.

## J5. Delta scaling and the scalar source profile
For delta>0, log softplus(delta,t)=log delta + H(t/delta). Ordinary constant/linear composition gives its actual j-th derivative, j≥1, as delta^(-j) H^(j)(t/delta). Since logSlope(delta,t)=delta^(-1) A(t/delta), J4 gives |D_t^j log softplus(delta,t)|≤C_j logSlope(delta,t)^j. The additive log-radius multiplier does not affect derivatives. Multiplication by p yields p C_j logSlope^j; for p≥1, p≤p^j.

## J6. Composition with fixed depth and common geometry
Fix one common L from the uniform reference-depth concavity result, then obtain all derivative bounds for this same depth u=referenceDepth L and all metric comparisons over [0,1]×K. The true Faà di Bruno formula expresses every order j derivative of logProfile(delta,c,p,u) as a finite sum of D_t^k log softplus times products of depth derivatives whose orders sum to j, with 1≤k≤j. Depth derivatives up to eight have compact bounds independent of delta,p,lambda. The scalar slope has a fixed positive lower bound a0, and the true depth metric covector norm has fixed positive lower bound m. Hence a^k≤a^j max(1,a0^(-j)) and beta=p a |du|≥p a m. This bounds each coordinate derivative by a constant beta^j, uniformly in delta,lambda,p≥1. Covariant derivatives differ by a finite sum of lower coordinate derivatives multiplied by bounded connection jets; beta has a fixed positive lower bound, so those lower powers are likewise bounded by beta^j. Actual connection jets must be derived from the fixed smooth reference metric; a generic implication with assumed bounds is not the source application.

## J7. Radius and beta consequences
The true radius equals R exp(p log softplus∘u). Higher coordinate derivatives of radius follow the ordinary exponential Faà di Bruno formula and J6, yielding |D^j r|≤C'_j r beta^j. The true beta equals p a(u)b_lambda, where b_lambda is the smooth positive depth metric norm. Its derivatives up to the orders required by the operator estimates follow J5, compact bounds for b_lambda, and the positive lower bound m. Therefore |D^j beta|≤C''_j beta^(j+1); differentiating beta^-1 yields |D^j beta^-1|≤C'''_j beta^(j-1). These conclusions still require actual formal chain/product/reciprocal bridges; they are not granted as premises by this expansion.

# Section 5: full adjoints, exact base cancellations and uniform form bounds

Author: section5_full_adjoint, 9 October 2026. This is an expanded derivation, not an independent verdict or canonical acceptance. It extends the previously authored v010 coefficient calculation by deriving the covariant full adjoint explicitly and by separating every analytic realization obligation. Frozen target v002, its definitions, all source authorities and library/checker pins remain unchanged. No original coercivity or density result is introduced as a premise.

Selected manuscript authority: original `04-shrinking-balls.tex`, SHA-256 `51bb060d379a819d6ae7b50415b8926bfd3c9f273423b454411e90659283cd44`, and `05-angular-estimate.tex`, SHA-256 `dee56e58ab1316aaebb7d53f48231658899ff07750fc7ab83f4cdd46ce3c1413`. In Section 5 the reference base density is mu=rho_gamma=sqrt(det gamma). It is not the transferred sphere density psi. The exact source coefficient is a=r Q_second, not r gamma^-1.

## FA1. Covariant integration against the full measure

Let Y be the fixed relatively compact base region and S_gamma Y its tangent sphere bundle. Work first with smooth sphere sections supported in a fixed compact subset of Y. The connection preserves the fiber probability measure. For a local orthonormal frame e_i, scalar base integration by parts gives

    integral <nabla_e_i u,v> dV_gamma d sigma
      = -integral <u,nabla_e_i v+(div_gamma e_i)v> dV_gamma d sigma.

The divergence term is mandatory. One cannot regard every orthonormal frame vector as a constant coordinate derivative. In coordinate trivializations the corresponding formula is partial_i^dagger=-partial_i-mu^-1 partial_i mu. These are two descriptions of the same full-density adjunction. Smooth compact base support removes the base boundary term. The probability normalization does not remove the factor mu.

The harmonic extension derivative A is a parallel covector-valued angular operator. Thus

    nabla_e_i(A_i v) = A_i nabla_e_i v + A_(nabla_e_i e_i) v.

Metric compatibility gives the exact frame identity

    sum_i (div_gamma e_i)e_i = -sum_i nabla_e_i e_i.

Indeed div e_i=sum_j<nabla_e_j e_i,e_j>=-sum_j<e_i,nabla_e_j e_j>, and expanding the right vector in the orthonormal frame proves the equality. Hence the extra tensor derivative and frame divergence cancel after summation. Therefore the full adjoint of sum_i A_i* nabla_e_i is precisely -sum_i A_i nabla_e_i. No frame-divergence remainder has been discarded. This calculation is equivalently covariant divergence of the indexed section A v; the covector index must remain in that notation.

**Formal status:** actual smooth R3 Hilbert-valued directional integration is proved in BaseDensityAdjoint. The tangent sphere connection, preservation of d sigma, parallel A and induced indexed connection are still to be realized. These are application obligations, not assumed new trusted facts.

## FA2. The angular adjoint and the one-degree correction

At fixed y, B is self-adjoint and equals k on H_k. The ambient harmonic derivative A_i maps H_k into H_(k-1); its sphere adjoint A_i* raises one degree. Consequently

    B A_i = A_i B - A_i,
    B A_i* = A_i* B + A_i*.

The first identity follows degree by degree and extends to smooth sections by convergence of their spherical harmonic series in the relevant finite Sobolev norms. A_i* is the sphere adjoint only; it does not include a base adjoint.

With T=sum_i A_i*(nabla_i+f_i B), FA1 gives

    T^dagger = -sum_i A_i nabla_i + sum_i f_i B A_i,
    T^flat   = -sum_i A_i nabla_i + sum_i f_i A_i B,
    Z=T^flat-T^dagger=sum_i f_i A_i.

Multiplication by the scalar f_i commutes with angular operators. There is no derivative of f in the adjoint of its zero-base term. On input degree k, the adjoint applies A_i first, so B then acts at degree k-1. This is the exact origin of Z.

For later symbol arguments these are scalar operators on sphere functions despite their base indices. In a fixed orthonormal trivialization A_i=V_i+omega_i B, where V_i is tangential directional differentiation along e_i-omega_i omega. The sphere integration identity div_S(V_i)=-(n-1)omega_i yields A_i*=-V_i+(n-1)omega_i+B M_(omega_i). This is a direct representation of their scalar angular character. The source's degree definitions, rather than an arbitrary principal-symbol substitute, remain normative.

**Open realization:** actual fiber L2 pairing, spherical harmonic completeness and the identification of B Sobolev scales with classical angular symbol mapping spaces. Existing Fischer/coefficient lemmas supply finite-degree identities but do not automatically identify the sphere pairing or completed domains.

## FA3. The actual scalar base principal coefficient

In the source harmonic coordinate system, the second equation is a positive scalar multiple of its metric Laplacian. The original coordinate first derivative term vanishes because these are second-metric harmonic coordinates. Writing it in the reference connection therefore introduces drift

    b_2^k=Q_second^ij Gamma_gamma^k_ij.

Indeed Q^ij Hess_gamma(F)_ij+b_2^k partial_k F equals Q^ij partial_i partial_j F. Thus derivatives of b_2 need derivatives of Q and fixed reference Christoffel coefficients; there is no extra derivative of h hidden in a first-derivative second-metric drift. This statement uses the source's harmonic coordinate realization and remains to be linked to the frozen target's constructed charts.

Expanding the actual covariant P produces P=2T+U+J, with

    U=a^ij partial_i partial_j+B^i partial_i+C,
    a^ij=r Q_second^ij=a^ji real, angular independent.

The identity D_i^+(r^-1 A_j*)=r^-1 A_j* D_i^+ uses BOTH partial_i(r^-1)=-f_i r^-1 and [B,A_j*]=A_j*. The two contributions cancel exactly. The reference pure angular contraction vanishes because sum_i A_i* A_i*=0. The remaining pure angular term is (h^ij/r) A_i* A_j*.

With beta>=1, the actual source smallness and profile bounds give, for the needed derivatives j,

    |partial^j r| <= C_j r beta^j,
    |partial^j(r^-1)| <= C_j r^-1 beta^j,
    |partial^j(h/r)| <= C_j epsilon beta^j.

The last inequality follows by the full Leibniz formula, the actual bound |partial^ell h|<=epsilon r for every ell used, and beta>=1. In particular it does not divide an unweighted fixed small h bound by an arbitrarily vanishing radius.

The term classes, including one beta factor per coefficient derivative, are

    a: epsilon beta^-2 Psi^0,
    B: epsilon beta^-1 Psi^1,
    C: epsilon Psi^2,
    T^dagger=K^ell partial_ell+M:
       K: fixed Psi^1, M: beta Psi^2,
    Z: beta Psi^1,
    J: fixed Psi^1 with no base derivatives.

The first-base terms include 2rQ f B, 2h A*, rQ(E+F) and r b_2 plus connection terms. The zero-base terms include h/r, r f_i f_j B^2, r Hess(f) B and products of trace remainders. Cross terms A*F and b_2 A* have fixed Psi^1 size and belong to J. The size r beta^2<=epsilon makes r beta<=epsilon beta^-1 and r<=epsilon beta^-2. All coefficient derivatives obey the corresponding extra beta factors. The reference volume and frame coefficients have fixed smooth bounds and hence fit weaker beta-weighted allowances.

**Open realization:** full complete-symbol and smoothing seminorm estimates for actual E,F, their up-to-six base derivatives, actual Q/h/frame/chart data and profile jets through order eight. Abstract coefficient classes alone do not close these obligations. J's undifferentiated norm is the only J input to final absorption, so its beta-dependent derivative allowances cannot create a hidden J absorption factor if its actual undifferentiated bound is established.

## FA4. Full coordinate adjoint of U

In a fixed orthonormal sphere trivialization d sigma is fixed and the base measure is mu(y)dy. For smooth compact base sections,

    (B^i partial_i)^dagger v
       = -mu^-1 partial_i(mu (B^i)* v),
    (a^ij partial_i partial_j)^dagger v
       = mu^-1 partial_j partial_i(mu a^ij v),
    C^dagger=C*.

The second derivative order reverses. Symmetry a^ij=a^ji and dummy-index exchange give the ordinary displayed symmetric principal term. Expanding every product yields

    U^dagger-U=D^i partial_i+E,
    D^i=2mu^-1 partial_j(mu a^ij)-B^i-(B^i)*,
    E=mu^-1 partial_i partial_j(mu a^ij)
       -mu^-1 partial_i(mu (B^i)*)+C*-C.

The formulas include derivatives of mu, a and B*. The coordinate derivative acts on the whole operator-valued coefficient. In the actual scalar angular calculus, differentiation and star commute in the appropriate symbol/kernel topology. This is a realization obligation, not inferred merely from a bound on B at one base point.

Reality of a removes the adjoint's second-base difference. Angular independence then ensures a commutes with all angular coefficients. These are distinct uses. If a were angular independent but complex, a*-a could retain a second-base term; if it were real but an angular operator, the cubic commutator could survive.

The exact BaseDensityAdjoint Lean component proves the first two underlying weighted base identities for actual Hilbert-valued sections, retaining the whole mu*a product and reversed order. It does not prove the unbounded angular operator star calculus. Because mu is the actual smooth positive reference density on the fixed base, its inverse and finitely many logarithmic derivatives have fixed bounds; hence D lies in epsilon beta^-1 Psi^1 and E in epsilon Psi^2 with inherited derivative allowances.

## FA5. Norm comparison without discarding cross terms

For the compact smooth section v, expand both squared norms. The pure model terms give 4(||Tv||^2-||T^flat v||^2). Move only the cross pairings and U square through their genuine full adjoints. Substitute T^flat=T^dagger+Z. The remaining exact operator is

    E_err=2[T^dagger,U]+2[U^dagger,T]+[U^dagger,U]
            -2(UZ+(UZ)^dagger).

Thus

    ||(2T+U)v||^2-||(2T^flat+U^dagger)v||^2
      =4(||Tv||^2-||T^flat v||^2)+Re<E_err v,v>.

This is already represented by the accepted AngularAlgebra identity under its explicit adjoint hypotheses; FA1–FA4 describe the actual source application that must discharge them. In real quadratic forms [U^dagger,T]=[T^dagger,U]^dagger, so their real pairings agree. The same holds for UZ and its adjoint. Estimating a partner by this pairing identity avoids an unnecessary further explicit coefficient-adjoint expansion and its derivative budget.

## FA6. Exact expansion of the critical commutators

Put H=K^ell partial_ell+M. All products below are ordered angular products; partial coefficients are actual base derivatives. With a symmetric and angular independent, direct Leibniz expansion gives

    [K partial,a partial^2]
      =K^ell(partial_ell a^ij) partial_i partial_j
        -2a^ij(partial_i K^ell) partial_j partial_ell
        -a^ij(partial_i partial_j K^ell) partial_ell,
    [K partial,B partial]
      =[K^ell,B^i] partial_ell partial_i
        +K^ell(partial_ell B^i) partial_i
        -B^i(partial_i K^ell) partial_ell,
    [K partial,C]=[K^ell,C] partial_ell+K^ell(partial_ell C),
    [M,a partial^2]=-2a^ij(partial_i M) partial_j
                     -a^ij(partial_i partial_j M),
    [M,B partial]=[M,B^i] partial_i-B^i(partial_i M),
    [M,C]=[M,C].

The third-base coefficient of the first line is K^ell a^ij-a^ij K^ell=0 exactly; no estimate on a third derivative of v is needed. The nonexistent [M,a] partial^2 term vanishes for the same reason. Here the six groups, rather than a total-order slogan, exhaust every term.

Scalar angular principal symbols commute, so [Psi^m,Psi^n] belongs to Psi^(m+n-1). Therefore the second-base coefficients have epsilon beta^-1 Psi^1 size; the first-base coefficients have epsilon Psi^2 size; the zero-base coefficients have epsilon beta Psi^3 size. A single base derivative of a second-base coefficient lies in epsilon Psi^1. Lower angular orders are included in these upper classes.

For the quadratic perturbation use [U^dagger,U]=[D partial+E,U]. The same exact expansion applies with K=D,M=E. Its stronger classes are

    base 2: epsilon^2 beta^-2 Psi^1,
    base 1: epsilon^2 beta^-1 Psi^2,
    base 0: epsilon^2 Psi^3.

Because beta>=1 and epsilon<=1 these fit the required epsilon classes. Its third-base coefficient again vanishes since D commutes with scalar a. There is no fourth-base term because U^dagger-U already has base order one.

Finally

    UZ=(a^ij Z) partial_i partial_j
         +(2a^ij partial_i Z+B^j Z) partial_j
         +a^ij partial_i partial_j Z+B^i partial_i Z+CZ.

This has the same three required classes. The existing actual one-dimensional PrincipalCommutator proof verifies a special case of the first group for actual derivatives and noncommuting coefficient algebra; it does not yet supply all multi-directional tensor and angular realization identities.

## FA7. Weighted angular form estimate

At each base point let X be the combined H^(1/2) norm of coordinate first derivatives of v and W=||v||_(3/2). For an actual second-base term S^ij partial_i partial_j with S in epsilon beta^-1 Psi^1, one genuine full-density base integration gives

    integral <S^ij partial_i partial_j v,v> mu dy
       =-integral <S^ij partial_j v,partial_i v> mu dy
        -integral <mu^-1 partial_i(mu S^ij)partial_j v,v> mu dy.

The actual mapping Psi^1:H^(1/2)→H^(-1/2) bounds the first term by C epsilon beta^-1 X^2. The derivative coefficient belongs to epsilon Psi^1, and its pairing is bounded by C epsilon X W. This includes BOTH the measure derivative and the weight derivative; |d beta|<=C beta^2 gives |d(beta^-1)|<=C. No derivative of an assumed bounded beta upper envelope is used.

For first-base epsilon Psi^2 terms use Psi^2:H^(1/2)→H^(-3/2); their pairing is at most C epsilon X W. For zero-base epsilon beta Psi^3 terms use Psi^3:H^(3/2)→H^(-3/2); their pairing is at most C epsilon beta W^2. The H^(1/2)-H^(-3/2) dual pairing, rather than an L2 operator norm of an order-two operator, is essential here.

At every base point, 2XW<=beta^-1 X^2+beta W^2 because beta>0. Integrating gives

    |Re<E_err v,v>|<=C epsilon integral(beta^-1 X^2+beta W^2).

Horizontal and coordinate derivatives differ by a fixed angular first-order connection. Its H^(3/2)→H^(1/2) mapping gives

    beta^-1||partial v||_(1/2)^2
      <=2 beta^-1||nabla v||_(1/2)^2+C beta^-1||v||_(3/2)^2.

Since beta^-1<=beta, the last term is included in N(v)^2. A fixed finite atlas and partition add only first/zero-base terms in the same classes. Thus the claimed error form bound follows once the actual operator seminorm and integration-domain realization is supplied. There is no estimate on partial^2 v, no frequency-ratio restriction and no beta upper bound.

## FA8. Inclusive derivative budget

The following maxima follow from the explicit groups, not from multiplying broad total counts:

| Operation | a derivatives | B derivatives | C derivatives | Other derivatives |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| H-U commutator plus one final IBP only on its base-2 terms | 2 | 2 | 1 | K through 2; M through 2 |
| Forming D=V_1 and E=V_0 | 1 and 2 | 0 and 1 | 0 | mu through 2 |
| V-U commutator, including final base-2 IBP | 4 | 3 | 2 | mu through 4 |
| UZ and its base-2 final IBP | 1 | 1 | 0 | Z through 2 |

For the longest V-U path, E includes partial^2 a. The term -a partial^2 E uses a through four derivatives, but it has base degree ZERO, hence is not subsequently integrated by parts. The base-2 coefficients depend on D partial a, a partial D and [D,B]; differentiating them once uses a through three and B through two. One must not append a final integration by parts to every coefficient indiscriminately and falsely require a fifth or sixth derivative there.

These actual maxima lie within the source's five U coefficient derivatives. Constructing C differentiates a trace coefficient once; taking it through two derivatives needs the trace through three, while the conservative five-coefficient envelope needs the trace through six. The actual sixth derivative of a trace term containing f_i uses f through seven. Eight profile derivatives therefore cover this part of the construction. In harmonic coordinates b_2=Q Gamma_gamma, so there is no hidden extra h derivative. Angular differentiation never differentiates h(y); fixed smooth first-metric angular derivatives are background inputs, not infinitely many epsilon-small derivatives of h. The displayed budget is sufficient only if the actual finite symbol/kernel mapping seminorms depend on coefficient derivatives in exactly these prescribed ways; that standard calculus applicability still requires proof or reviewed precise literature interfaces.

## FA9. Absorption and uniform parameter order

Let the actual raising estimate supply c_R>0 independently of the shrinking parameter. Fix a finite error seminorm constant C_E for all the preceding coefficients, with the common profile constants independent of the lower threshold. Choose epsilon<=min(1,2c_R/C_E), and retain the nonnegative square on the comparison's left only long enough to derive

    N(v)<=C_R||(2T+U)v||.

The fixed J Psi^1 mapping gives ||Jv||<=C_J||v||_(H^1)<=C_J beta_0^-1 N(v). Choose beta_0 so C_R C_J/beta_0<=1/2. Then N(v)<=2C_R||Pv||. The geometry/common conformal L, fixed base/cutoff margins and background bounds precede these constants. With p,R_* and the positive cutoff separation r_min=R_* t_b^p fixed, restrict the common lambda range. Only then vary delta under H_8<=epsilon r_delta. Bounds may depend on p,R_*,t_b once fixed. Choosing lambda anew for each delta would not prove the source's uniform statement.

# Section 5 density equation and uniformity: complete application expansion

Prepared before new Lean implementation. This is a mathematical expansion and dependency audit target, not an assertion that the outstanding geometric/PDE premises have been formalized. Reference `05-angular-estimate.tex` SHA-256 `dee56e58ab1316aaebb7d53f48231658899ff07750fc7ab83f4cdd46ce3c1413` and `04-shrinking-balls.tex` in the preserved original manuscript reading copy.

## D1. Local functional, measure and normalization

Fix positive δ and an interior center y₀ with an allowed closed γ-normal ball. The continued mixed kernel is smooth on a neighborhood of its boundary and solves the first equation in x and the second equation in y there. For a first-metric harmonic u on a neighborhood of that closed ball, define the original outward first-metric Green flux T_y u. The sphere measure used to represent it is the probability measure dσ_y on the γ-unit tangent sphere, not the physical first-metric area measure.

For centers near y₀ choose one slightly larger surrounding surface inside the common kernel and u domains. Compactness and openness give a center neighborhood for which all moving spheres and intervening collars are inside this domain. Green's identity in x changes the flux to this fixed surface. The second operator in y can then pass under the fixed integral; both kernel terms solve it, including their first-variable normal derivatives. Thus F_u(y)=T_y u is second-metric harmonic locally. The center neighborhood may depend on u. This is a local argument for every such u; no approximation by global source-generated solutions is needed here.

The Dirichlet boundary operator and its sphere adjoint give the smooth representing density ψ, with the full physical flux factors retained before pulling back to dσ_y. Parallel transport preserves dσ_y. On the lower known region Green's identity gives T_y 1=1. The local harmonicity, connectedness and unique continuation propagate this identity, so ∫ψ dσ_y=1. The construction, Green identity, connectedness and unique continuation are explicit unresolved realization obligations; the normalization is not postulated for the final transfer construction.

## D2. First derivative and the order of the second product

Write U_u(y,ω)=u(exp_y^γ(r(y)ω)). Its actual trace equation is ∇_i U_u=C_i U_u. Use the sphere adjoint C_i*, and write D_i=∇_i+C_i*. Metric compatibility gives

    ∇_j F_u = <∇_j ψ,U_u> + <ψ,∇_j U_u>
              = <D_j ψ,U_u>.

Here D_j ψ carries a covector index j. Differentiate again with the induced connection on that index:

    (Hess_γ F_u)_ij = <∇_i(D_j ψ),U_u> + <D_j ψ,C_i U_u>
                    = <(∇_i+C_i*)(D_j ψ),U_u>.

In coordinates ∇_i(D_j ψ) includes the term −Γ^k_ij D_k ψ. Fiber connection terms also remain. Consequently the covariant product has exactly the order D_i D_j and does not mean applying two scalar coordinate derivatives with no covector correction. Contract only after differentiation. For the normalized second equation Q^ij(Hess_γ F_u)_ij+b₂^j∇_jF_u=0, Q stays outside this contraction; no derivative of Q is introduced by taking a base adjoint. The full base-and-sphere adjoints used later in coercivity are a different operation.

Therefore

    <Pψ,U_u>=0,
    P=r[Q^ij(∇_i+C_i*)(∇_j+C_j*)+b₂^i(∇_i+C_i*)].

All quantities here are at the same center, and r>0. This derivation retains the density's center dependence and the trace operator's derivatives. Formalizing this calculation must also justify the differentiations, pairing adjunction on smooth data, and induced tensor connection.

## D3. Density of the local harmonic traces

Fix the center and radius r₀>0, and let h be any smooth datum on its unit sphere. Choose slightly larger normal balls of radii τ=r₀+η, η>0, inside the relevant first-coordinate neighborhood. Pull their Dirichlet equations back to the closed unit ball by z↦exp_y^γ(τz), and prescribe h at its unit boundary. Denote the pulled-back solution v_τ. At these positive radii the operator family is smooth and uniformly elliptic, with invertible Dirichlet realization. Smooth parameter dependence in every fixed boundary regularity order gives v_τ→v_r₀ in C^m of the closed unit ball for every finite m.

The corresponding physical solution u_τ is harmonic on an open neighborhood of the original closed radius-r₀ ball. Its trace on the original sphere is v_τ((r₀/τ)ω), which tends to v_r₀(ω)=h in every C^m sphere norm. At y₀, D2 annihilates each of these traces. Since Pψ is smooth for fixed positive δ, its sphere pairing is continuous in these norms. It therefore annihilates every smooth h. Taking h=Pψ (real case) proves its squared norm is zero, hence Pψ=0. No common center neighborhood for all approximants is required. This uses a positive-radius Dirichlet parameter theorem; it does not yet require estimates uniform at radius zero.

## D4. Removing the constant mode

Let χ be the fixed smooth compactly base-supported cutoff from `balls:cutoff-region`, and set φ=χ(ψ−1). Its fiber integral is χ(1−1)=0, and its base support is compact. The operator P is linear and the commutator means [P,χ]w=P(χw)−χPw. Since Pψ=0,

    Pφ = −χP1 + [P,χ](ψ−1).

The decomposition P=2T+U+J must be established for the actual trace operators. The raising part T kills 1. In U=Σ_|α|≤2 U_α∂^α, all terms with nonzero base derivative kill 1; U₀∈εΨ² gives a uniformly bounded U₀1. J∈Ψ¹ gives a uniformly bounded J1. Thus P1 is uniformly bounded after the fixed structural choices. The size statement for U₀ is essential: merely expanding r f_i f_j B² without using rβ²≤ε would not give the required uniform bound.

## D5. The cutoff commutator and its two regions

Since χ is independent of ω, [J,χ]=0. The principal second base term is precisely rQ^ij∂_i∂_j, so its commutator contributes

    2rQ^ij(∂_iχ)(∂_jw) + rQ^ij(∂_i∂_jχ)w.

The symmetry of Q is used in the factor 2. The raising term contributes 2Σ_i A_i*(∇_iχ)w. The first-base coefficients of U contribute bounded order-one angular operators applied to w, while its base-zero part commutes with χ. Fixed connection/trivialization coefficients and cutoff derivatives remain bounded. The claimed estimate is

    ||[P,χ]w|| ≤ Cχ(||w||_{L²(S;H¹_fiber)}+||r∇w||_{L²(S×sphere)}),

where S is a fixed small neighborhood containing the supports of every nonzero derivative of χ. Derivative supports can be kept inside the union of the two open regions below by fixed margins in the cutoff construction. Cχ must depend only on fixed geometry, symbol seminorms and the chosen cutoff, never on δ or allowed sufficiently small λ.

On the lower region y_n<−1/4, the functional is ordinary evaluation. Its representing density is the normalized Poisson density at the center of the rescaled unit-ball problem. The rescaled family is smooth uniformly elliptic down to r=0. Uniform parameter estimates for this normalized evaluation density imply bounds on its angular norms and partial center/radius derivatives. Composing r(y) introduces ∇r, bounded by the fixed metric comparison and rβ; the condition rβ²≤ε with β≥β₀≥1 controls it. This assertion concerns the normalized Poisson density, not the unscaled Green kernel or its singular flux factors separately.

On the other region t>t_b>0, softplus satisfies ℓ_δ(t)≥t_b, hence r≥r_min=R_*t_b^p>0. The fixed p,R_*,t_b are chosen before δ and the final small-λ cutoff. The radius also has a fixed upper bound, and all finitely required radius derivatives there are uniformly bounded; exponential tails in t/δ control δ→0. The mixed kernel's fixed-positive-separation estimates and the actual Dirichlet/sphere construction then give the required ψ and first-base bounds. Those bounds may depend on r_min and thus on p,R_*,t_b, which are fixed. Compactness and a finite cover combine the two region estimates. Existence/compatibility of this mixed kernel, and the uniform parameter estimates for both constructions, remain open formal obligations.

## D6. Uniform coercivity and the final bound

Assume the actual full moving-trace coercivity has been proved with fixed C_coer:

    N(φ) ≤ C_coer ||Pφ||

for every smooth compactly base-supported zero-fiber-mean φ. No such original result is accepted as a literature premise. Its norm contains β²||φ||_{H¹_fiber}²; β≥β₀≥1 implies ||φ||_{L²}≤β₀⁻¹N(φ). By D4–D5 the right-hand side is bounded by some fixed A independent of δ and all sufficiently small λ satisfying the coefficient bootstrap. Hence

    ||χψ|| ≤ ||φ||+||χ|| ≤ β₀⁻¹ C_coer A+||χ||.

The norm of χ is also uniformly bounded: γ_λ and its volume measure range over a compact smooth family on the fixed support, and dσ_y is probability measure. This proves the application once every stated obligation is realized. It does not itself prove coercivity, the actual density construction, or the coefficient bootstrap for arbitrarily small δ. ## D7. Parameter and proof-status ledger

## P1. Actual fixed background family

Fix the admissible first metric g, one common real L and a compact coordinate set K. Define gamma_lambda=referenceMetric(dilatedMetric g lambda,L), rho_lambda=vol gamma_lambda and q_lambda=gamma_lambda^-1. These are the actual conformal reference objects, not an exterior-admissibility assertion about gamma. Joint smoothness in (lambda,x) follows from the exact conformal identities

    rho_lambda(x)=exp(-3L referenceCoordinateDepth(x))*vol g(lambda*x),
    q_lambda(x)_ij=exp(2L referenceCoordinateDepth(x))*(g(lambda*x)^-1)_ij.

Both are smooth for every lambda and x. Actual positivity of gamma gives rho>0, so its inverse is jointly smooth too. Restrict lambda to [0,1] and x to K. The finite sum of absolute values of rho, rho^-1, all q entries and their first/second actual coordinate derivatives is continuous on this compact product. Its bound supplies one M>=1 for all those quantities. M depends only on g,L,K and the fixed coordinate directions, and is chosen before delta,R,p,epsilon. This directly supplies rho^-1 and rho derivative bounds; no density derivative is discarded.

## P2. Exact coefficient and derivative identities

At a fixed lambda and matrix index i,j, write q=q_lambda, mu=rho_lambda, and h=h_ij. The actual source coefficient is a=r*(q+h); its weighted coefficient is c=mu*a=mu*r*(q+h). It is never replaced by r*q and there is no cancellation of D(mu*h).

Let D_i denote the true fixed-coordinate Frechet directional derivative. All functions are actual smooth functions. The exact product rules give

    D_i c=(D_i r)*mu*(q+h)
            +r*((D_i mu)*(q+h)+mu*(D_i q+D_i h)),

and, with b=mu*(q+h),

    D_jD_i c=(D_jD_i r)*b+(D_i r)*(D_j b)
                  +(D_j r)*(D_i b)+r*(D_jD_i b),
    D_jD_i b=(D_jD_i mu)*(q+h)
                  +(D_i mu)*(D_j q+D_j h)
                  +(D_j mu)*(D_i q+D_i h)
                  +mu*(D_jD_i q+D_jD_i h).

Every Dmu,Dr,Dh term is retained. The helper hypotheses on h are precisely actual local coordinate smallness: |h|,|D_i h|,|D_jD_i h|<=epsilon*r at the point. These are a subset of the source H8 assumption, not new assumptions for main.

## P3. Uniform quantitative estimates

Assume beta>=1, r>0, 0<=epsilon<=1 and r*beta^2<=epsilon. Then r<=1 and epsilon*r<=1. The fixed background bound M gives

    |b|<=M*(M+1),
    |D_i b|<=2M*(M+1),
    |D_jD_i b|<=4M*(M+1).

Actual radius bounds are |D_i r|<=J1*r*beta and |D_jD_i r|<=J2*r*beta^2, with J1,J2 fixed independently of lambda,delta,R,p after g,L,K are fixed. Existing actual reference-radius jet results supply them; the component may first prove a generic actual-function estimate and retain its exact application separately if the bounded work window is tight.

The complete derivative identities then imply

    |D_i(mu*a)|<=(J1+2)*M*(M+1)*epsilon/beta,
    |D_jD_i(mu*a)|<=(J2+4J1+4)*M*(M+1)*epsilon.

Here r*beta<=epsilon/beta follows by multiplying r*beta^2<=epsilon by beta^-1, and all lower beta powers are dominated because beta>=1. Constants are fixed before the shrinking parameter.

## P4. Actual formal-adjoint defect

For the actual symmetric scalar matrix a and positive mu, the already checked ScalarBaseAdjoint theorem gives

    U2^dagger-U2=mu^-1 sum_ij D_jD_i(mu*a_ij)
                     +2mu^-1 sum_ij D_j(mu*a_ij) D_i,

with actual smooth section argument in each term. Matrix symmetry is a genuine local property of Q_gamma+h, not a consequence of arbitrary h smallness. # Density of the actual positive harmonic core in the mean kernel

Prepared before implementation. This concerns Hilbert-space density of
positive-degree harmonic traces, not Section 5's still-open uniform density
estimate for the mixed-kernel equation. It uses only the precise reviewed
ordinary orthogonality and harmonic-span density parameters from ABR5.9/5.12.

## D1. Actual constant direction

Let e be the genuine L2 trace of C(1), and P the algebraic supremum of the
actual degree k+1 trace subspaces. The actual probability integral pairing
gives inner(e,e)=1, hence the continuous mean functional takes e to1. A
degree-zero homogeneous polynomial is exactly its constant coefficient;
therefore the degree-zero image subspace is precisely the real span of e.
The orthogonal complement of that span is exactly the earlier mean kernel.

## D2. Positive span and constants

The checked positive-degree orthogonality gives P <= meanZeroSphere.
Consequently e is orthogonal to P. Every vector v orthogonal to P admits
w=v-mean(v)e. The mean of w is zero, and w remains orthogonal to P, by real
linearity of pairing and orthogonality of e.

## D3. Exhaustion argument

The preceding w is orthogonal to every actual harmonic degree: degree zero
uses its zero mean and D1, and positive degree uses its membership in P's
orthogonal complement. Thus w is orthogonal to the supremum of all degrees.
ABR's explicit dense-span parameter and continuity of pairing imply w is
orthogonal to the whole true Hilbert space. Taking its own pairing shows
w=0. Therefore P's orthogonal complement is exactly the real span of e.

## D4. Closed mean-zero core

The actual L2 space is complete. The checked Hilbert theorem that the double
orthogonal complement equals topological closure, applied to D3, gives
closure(P)=span(e)^orthogonal=meanZeroSphere. This is a genuine dense-core

    rho_lambda(x)=exp(-3L referenceCoordinateDepth(x))*vol g(lambda*x),
    q_lambda(x)_ij=exp(2L referenceCoordinateDepth(x))*(g(lambda*x)^-1)_ij.

Both are smooth for every lambda and x. Actual positivity of gamma gives rho>0, so its inverse is jointly smooth too. Restrict lambda to [0,1] and x to K. The finite sum of absolute values of rho, rho^-1, all q entries and their first/second actual coordinate derivatives is continuous on this compact product. Its bound supplies one M>=1 for all those quantities. M depends only on g,L,K and the fixed coordinate directions, and is chosen before delta,R,p,epsilon. This directly supplies rho^-1 and rho derivative bounds; no density derivative is discarded.

At a fixed lambda and matrix index i,j, write q=q_lambda, mu=rho_lambda, and h=h_ij. The actual source coefficient is a=r*(q+h); its weighted coefficient is c=mu*a=mu*r*(q+h). It is never replaced by r*q and there is no cancellation of D(mu*h).

Let D_i denote the true fixed-coordinate Frechet directional derivative. All functions are actual smooth functions. The exact product rules give

    D_i c=(D_i r)*mu*(q+h)
            +r*((D_i mu)*(q+h)+mu*(D_i q+D_i h)),

and, with b=mu*(q+h),

    D_jD_i c=(D_jD_i r)*b+(D_i r)*(D_j b)
                  +(D_j r)*(D_i b)+r*(D_jD_i b),
    D_jD_i b=(D_jD_i mu)*(q+h)
                  +(D_i mu)*(D_j q+D_j h)
                  +(D_j mu)*(D_i q+D_i h)
                  +mu*(D_jD_i q+D_jD_i h).

Every Dmu,Dr,Dh term is retained. The helper hypotheses on h are precisely actual local coordinate smallness: |h|,|D_i h|,|D_jD_i h|<=epsilon*r at the point. These are a subset of the source H8 assumption, not new assumptions for main.

# Pinned determinant derivative: upfront dependency expansion

This packet compiles an exact copy of the pinned Tau Ceti determinant module in the private development workspace; no runtime library, checker or pin is modified. Original source is `.runtime/calderon-v002/TauCeti/TauCeti/Analysis/Calculus/FDeriv/Det.lean`, SHA-256 `4b7e8cac3fed0ddf79947e845fa2fc5e9477e8152744a0c9f02ecb77e9e58864`.

The three declarations prove the line derivative det(I+tB)' at zero equals trace B, differentiability of det by its finite permutation sum, and the genuine Frechet derivative at identity equals the trace continuous linear map. The line formula comes from the checked characteristic-polynomial coefficient identity. Differentiability upgrades it to equality of continuous linear maps by evaluating on every direction B. The operator matrix norm is explicitly used. This dependency supports the already expanded positive metric volume/trace route; it is not a literature premise or a proof of angular coercivity. A later generalization at invertible M uses det(Y)=det(M)det(M⁻¹Y) and genuine differentiation of left multiplication. Finite-dimensional norm/entry derivative matching must be proved explicitly when applying it to the actual scalar-entry-smooth metric field.

Private compilation, replay and printed root axioms are development evidence, separate from canonical acceptance. Do not add this module to the configured runtime pin during ordinary proof work.
